sources.title: Building effective agents
findings: Separates workflows, where code orchestrates LLM calls along predefined paths, from agents, where the LLM directs its own process and tool use.
Names the augmented LLM building block and the patterns prompt chaining, routing, parallelization (sectioning, voting), orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer.
Agents are LLMs using tools on environmental feedback in a loop; they may pause for human checkpoints and carry stopping conditions such as a maximum iteration count.

Advises starting with plain LLM API calls, adding complexity only when simpler setups fall short, and giving tool definitions as much prompt-engineering care as prompts (the agent-computer interface).
Warns that frameworks add abstraction layers that hide prompts and responses and invite needless complexity.
sources.limits: Vendor engineering guidance from late 2024; a page note says much of the tooling landscape has changed since. Not a controlled study.

sources.title: Your AI Product Needs Evals
findings: Describes fast, cheap assertions as the first level of evals, run on every code change.
Says to read traces and keep looking at data; examine as much as possible at first and sample more later.
sources.limits: Single practitioner's experience; opinionated, not a controlled study.

sources.title: LLM Evals: Everything You Need to Know (evals FAQ)
findings: Error analysis is open coding of traces into notes, then axial coding into a failure taxonomy with counts per category.
Prefers binary pass/fail judgments over 1-5 scales for clearer labels and smaller samples.
An LLM judge is validated against human labels, using its true positive and true negative rates, before its scores are trusted.
Generic metrics such as a hallucination score rarely capture what matters; build application-specific evaluators.
For most teams one domain expert sets the quality standard.
sources.limits: The authors call these sharp opinions about what works in most cases, not universal rules; they also sell a course.

sources.title: Model Context Protocol specification, overview (2025-11-25)
findings: Servers offer resources, prompts, and tools; clients may offer sampling, roots, and elicitation.
Users must consent to data access and tool invocation; tool descriptions and annotations are untrusted unless from a trusted server.
sources.limits: The page served for the latest version was read; the version moves, so re-read the current one.

sources.title: MCP specification: tools (2025-11-25)
findings: Tools are model-controlled; there should always be a human in the loop able to deny a tool call.
Execution errors return isError with actionable text the model can use to retry; protocol errors are different and less recoverable.
sources.limits: Specification text for one dated version.

sources.title: MCP specification: sampling (2025-11-25)
findings: Sampling lets a server request an LLM call through the client, nested in its own features, without holding model keys.
There should be a human in the loop able to deny sampling requests.
sources.limits: Specification text for one dated version.

sources.title: MCP specification: roots (2025-11-25)
findings: Roots are the filesystem locations a client tells a server it may operate in, usually set through workspace configuration.
sources.limits: Specification text for one dated version.

sources.title: MCP specification: elicitation (2025-11-25)
findings: Elicitation lets a server ask the user for input, in form mode or URL mode.
Servers must not request passwords, keys, tokens, or payment credentials in form mode; sensitive interactions use URL mode.
sources.limits: Specification text for one dated version.

sources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents (agent context techniques)
findings: Context rot: as tokens in the window grow, recall of that context falls, so context is a finite attention budget with diminishing returns.
Just-in-time context: agents keep lightweight identifiers (file paths, stored queries, links) and load data through tools at runtime instead of pre-loading everything.
Compaction summarizes a conversation near the window limit and restarts from the summary, keeping decisions and unresolved bugs; clearing old tool results is the lightest form.
Structured note-taking persists notes outside the window and reads them back later, tracking progress across long tasks.
Sub-agents work in clean windows and return a condensed summary (often 1,000 to 2,000 tokens), isolating detailed search context from the lead agent.
Aim for the minimal set of high-signal tokens; tools are the contract with the environment and should be token efficient with minimal overlap.
sources.limits: Vendor engineering guidance from experience, not a controlled study; the same page is registered for its prompt-writing findings as SRC-WRITE-050 in the writing registry.
